_TEMPLATE: ARCS 6-TAB WAR-ROOM. The disciplined internal method behind ahmed.arcs.care, parameterized.
_HOW_TO_USE: 2. Fill every {{PLACEHOLDER}} and each block's content. Delete blocks/tabs you don't need.
3. Tag each field/block audience:'internal' (default, war-room only) or 'both' (safe to share).
6. Wire the subdomain in next.config.ts + vercel domains add; gate internal with a NON-guessable pw.
_METHOD: Six tabs = six disciplines in sequence. PRE-CALL: orient before contact (True North, register/intent, intel, questions, landmines). EX-ANTE: file a decision receipt BEFORE the event (hypothesis + predicted Y-gate + pre-committed move + falsifier) so you can be scored later. FORGE: pressure-test the brief's own claims against external substrates via an independent skeptic (grounded / inference / struck). RECOIL: after the event, close the receipt — belief-update ledger (confidence x conviction), kairos/quiet-signals, risk flags, next steps. WAR GAME: adversarial + kinematic — measured manifold, BAR/LAB/COURT gauntlet, ATG pre-mortem on the critical path vs their real objections. DEFENSIBILITY: translate the method into the counterpart's native register (Rosetta) + a 5-verb x 4-proofing matrix + the antifragile-core / lossless-translation test.

header.title: Contract OS · Staff Product Manager
header.sub: How I own an AI product and plan its roadmap, for Dioptra.

p: Before and after every conversation that matters, I keep a working file. This is the one I kept for last week's call, with one change: my notes about people are removed. What is left is the method: what I predicted, how I checked my own reads against what was actually said, and what I changed my mind about.

It is the same discipline I would bring to Contract OS. Write the prediction down before the event, check it afterward against something outside my own head, and keep the corrections visible instead of smoothing them over.

Short version for Farah: sections 2 to 4 are what I would own, my first 30 days and how the work is checked, about a two-minute read. Sections 5 to 8 are the method behind it, one step each, if you want it.

blocks.h2: The prediction, filed before the call

fields.label: The question
fields.value: Is this a real product-ownership seat, and can I make the case for it without revenue proof?

fields.label: What I expect to see
fields.value: I get asked for revenue proof early.

fields.label: Belief I held least firmly

p: Without a written prediction, every outcome looks like what I expected. With one, I find out how often I am right, and the misses teach me more than the hits. It is the same rule I use for a release: the pass rules are frozen before the benchmark runs.

After the call I wrote down how I thought it went, then went back over the call and checked each read against what was actually said, not my memory of it. Grounded means what was said forces it. Inference means it is my read and nothing forces it. Struck means I overreached, and the read is corrected.

blocks.h2: What I changed my mind about
blocks.intro: What moved for me after we spoke.

items.html: The seat. I came in framing the role as part product owner, part forward-deployed engineer. I now read the seat as owning the product Farah has been carrying: sorting the feature requests the enablement lawyers bring back, and staying in front of customers with quick prototypes and demos. The forward-deployed engineering already sits with your legal engineers.
Revenue. I expected to be pressed for revenue proof early. I was not, and the numbers I offered were not revenue numbers anyway. It is still the gap I would name first, so it stays on my list.
My own read of the call. I was more confident in my post-call notes than what was actually said allowed. I now treat my first read of any conversation as a draft.

p: The corrections are the most useful output. Pitching myself as part forward-deployed engineer would have missed, because that work already has an owner. An error like that is cheap to fix before the next conversation and expensive after it.

blocks.h2: What AI product have I owned, and how did I plan the roadmap?
p: The AI product I have owned end to end is ARCS, a decision tool that labels every claim confirmed or unconfirmed. A user brings a consequential question. An LLM pipeline returns a recommendation with its reasoning, what is confirmed, what is not, and a confidence state.

I built it with Claude Code agents as my engineering team. Agents do what the spec says, not what I meant, so I write the acceptance test first. What I have not had is a human engineer pushing back on a decision; I expect Dioptra's team to.

What ARCS does not prove yet is the revenue side. With Contract OS I would tie every roadmap bet to revenue: a request more than one customer shares, a shorter sale, or an expansion, and learn which bets travel through Icertis's customers and which through Dioptra's own deals.

blocks.h2: Four decisions that shaped the roadmap
blocks.intro: Each with the reason it exists.

items.html: Code, not the model, applies the confidence rule. Code maps the model's reported signals plus the user's stated stakes to a state. The model still supplies most of those inputs; checking them against something outside the model is the next step.
Trust is in the data model. Each answer stores its confirmed and unconfirmed claims and its computed state, so a user can reopen it later and see why. A claim nothing can verify stays unconfirmed.
Success is defined before shipping. Pass rules are frozen before a benchmark runs. Two of my own predictions were wrong, and the benchmark caught both.
Saying no is on the roadmap. The backlog records what is deliberately not built and why.

blocks.h2: How it is enforced, with real numbers

rows.v: I set the pass bar before testing, I report the misses, and two of my own bets failed and did not ship.

One pre-registered benchmark, run once, pass bars set first: 10 checks, 8 passed, 2 failed. The text index needed more than 85% and scored exactly 85%, so it failed; a prefilter failed too. Neither was adopted. The one new feature, a lineage index, shipped only after clearing its bar: about 70% faster, one run.
No confident wrong answers in 800 test questions I wrote, so the true rate is likely under about 0.4%.
Every change I ship is logged and cannot be quietly edited later.
Not yet measured end to end in ARCS. The one timing I have is a lookup cut from 5.15 s to 1.55 s. This is what I would learn from your team first.
Pre-registration and every result, failures included, are available on request.

blocks.h2: What I would do first on Contract OS
blocks.intro: A proposal to test, not a plan to impose.

items.html: Weeks 1 to 2: In DUMBO five days a week from day one. agree with Farah which decisions move to me first and which stay with her. Sit on customer calls with the legal engineers and trace one contract end to end through the systems that customer actually uses. By the end of week 1, a first sort of the open feature requests into build, process and wait, for Farah to mark up.
Week 3: learn how accuracy and unauthorized action rate are measured today, and who owns each eval.
Week 4: one written decision doc, argued with the founders before it is a decision: the next bet, which customers' requests it answers at once, the revenue it moves, and what we will not build.

blocks._doc: GAUNTLET: BAR (ruin edge) / LAB (Loki/Advisor/Bayesian) / COURT (constitutional) / red-blue-steel.
blocks.intro: Adversarial pass on the opportunity, not the person.

items.html: BAR (ruin): the commute. A 5-day onsite at roughly an hour each way is the edge most likely to fail after an offer, not before.
LAB · Loki: Doug's "really interesting background" is a talent lead's courtesy. The real gate is Farah reading Doug's summary, and that summary is probably "consultant with his own AI tool."
LAB · Bayesian: a warm recruiter screen with a named next step is a moderate signal. Prior 0.55 to about 0.62, not higher until Farah books.
COURT: counterpart-facing words stay plain: no ARCS, Manana Sprints or decision-receipt vocabulary. This file stays internal.

blocks._doc: ANTIFRAGILE CORE + LOSSLESS-TRANSLATION TEST. Prove being-wrong is the feature, then restate the whole thing in their vocabulary with zero loss.
p: The corrections are the most useful output. Pitching myself as part forward-deployed engineer would have failed in front of Farah, because her legal engineers already do that work. My own post-call read was wrong twice (the onsite hedge, trust never discussed), and an independent re-read caught it. Both kinds of error are cheap to fix before the next call and expensive after it.

Lossless test, in their words: I sort the feature requests your enablement lawyers bring back, decide what gets built, what becomes process and what waits, and I check each decision later against what customers actually used.
